deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft for Riemann's Inauguraldissertation (1851), in the part that applies the Dirichlet-principle results of the previous articles (no interior maximum or minimum, uniqueness, etc.) to conformal mapping.

Header paragraph (heavily struck). Riemann remarks that the boundary-value determinations of the preceding articles can also be applied to lines in the interior of T. For the values of du/dp and ds he says one extra datum is needed. That datum is a closed line returning into itself, along which the values are prescribed, together with a starting point (where s attains its smallest value). This is a fragment about fixing the additive constant and the starting point of the arc length. Most of it is cancelled.

Main derivation (below the horizontal rule).

Setting (my reading). A complex function of z is given; its logarithmic derivative log(du/dz) is used. Near a winding point (Windungspunkt) z' of order n-1, the quantity log(du/dz) - (n-1)log(z-z') stays finite. Write u also for the real part of log(du/dz), as Riemann does.

1. Away from the winding points, u is everywhere determinate and continuous, and it is harmonic. By Green's theorem, the integral of du/dp ds over the whole boundary of T, together with small boundaries around each winding point, is 0. Here p is Riemann's normal pointing into the region. Hence the boundary integral of T equals minus the sum of the integrals around the winding points.

2. At a winding point put z - z' = rho e^{i phi}. Then u - (n-1)log rho tends to a finite limit. The difference u - (n-1)log rho is regular and harmonic near z'. Therefore the integral of d/dp[u - (n-1)log rho] ds around the small enclosing boundary is 0, i.e. ∫ du/dp ds = (n-1)∫ d(log rho)/dp ds.

3. On a small circle about z' the normal is radial, ds = rho dphi and d(log rho)/drho = 1/rho. So (n-1)∫_0^{2pi} (d log rho/d rho) rho dphi = (n-1)2pi in absolute value. With the orientation conventions this gives a contribution -(n-1)2pi to the boundary integral of T.

4. Summing over all winding points: the integral of du/dp ds over the whole boundary of T equals -2pi Σ(n-1) = -2pi ν, where ν is the sum of the orders of the winding points. The same holds for any part of T containing all the winding points.

5. Last (partly struck) lines. The boundary element ds of T is mapped to an element dσ of the image surface S, and an element dπ is written as dσ e^{psi i}, with psi an angle. This prepares the interpretation of ∫ du/dp ds as the total turning of the tangent direction of the image boundary.

Interpretation. The boundary integral of du/dp equals the total change of arg(du/dz) along the boundary. So the page proves that the winding (turning) of the derivative along the boundary counts the branch points with multiplicity, ν = Σ(n-1). This is the argument principle applied to the derivative of a conformal map: a boundary-rotation / Riemann–Hurwitz-type count. It is used to relate the tangent turning of the image boundary to the number of winding points.
errors: Sign bookkeeping is loose. With z - z' = rho e^{i phi}, (n-1)∫_0^{2pi}(d log rho/d rho) rho dphi equals +2pi(n-1), not -2pi(n-1). The minus sign appears only after taking the normal p pointing into T, which on the small circle points toward or away from z' depending on convention, and transferring the term to the outer boundary. The written chain '= (n-1)∫... = -(n-1)2pi' therefore hides a sign change (or a struck-out minus).

Integrating phi only over 0..2pi presupposes that z is the single-sheeted (uniformizing) variable at the winding point. If z were the coordinate on the multi-sheeted surface, phi would run over 0..2n pi and the singular coefficient would be (n-1)/n. The page's statement is consistent only with the derivative du/dz having a zero of order n-1 in a single-valued variable z.
The extra condition in the header paragraph (closed line plus initial point) is stated incompletely and largely cancelled; it is not a complete argument.

results.what: Boundary integral of the normal derivative of log|f'| (the boundary turning of arg f') equals -2pi times the sum of the orders of the critical (winding) points, proved via Green's theorem with small circles excised around the singularities.
results.modern_name: Argument principle for f' / turning-number (Umlaufsatz) relation with branch points; local Riemann–Hurwitz-type count
results.usually_credited_to: Argument principle: Cauchy (1831/1855). Branch-point counting for Riemann surfaces: Riemann (1851/1857), Hurwitz (1891).

results.what: Removal of a logarithmic singularity of a harmonic function by subtracting (n-1)log rho, and evaluating flux through a small circle as 2pi(n-1).
results.modern_name: Flux of fundamental solution / Gauss–Green with logarithmic singularity
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Green; standard in Riemann's dissertation

deep.surprise_reason: This is draft material for Riemann's 1851 dissertation, where branch-point counting and Green's-theorem arguments with logarithmic singularities appear in published form. The computation is a standard argument-principle style count and is well known to be in Riemann's circle of ideas.

checkable.asserts: Flux of log rho through a circle of radius rho is 2pi (the expression equals 0).
log rho is harmonic away from the origin (result 0).
For f = z^n, log f' - (n-1)log z is constant (finite), i.e. z=0 is a winding point of order n-1 in Riemann's sense.
Winding of arg f' around a circle about a zero of f' of order n-1 equals 2pi i (n-1); intended to evaluate to 4*pi*I for n=3 (substitute z=exp(I*t) before integrating).

transcription_corrections: 'Bedeutung aber log du/dz ...' should read 'Bedeutet aber' or more likely 'Bekommt aber'; the sense is 'If log(du/dz) - (n-1)log(z-z') has a finite value (Nach Def.)'.
In 'findet sich nun ∫du/dp ds = (n-1)∫_0^{2pi}...', the image shows a struck symbol before (n-1). A sign is likely involved; trust the image over the plain '(n-1)'.
'1. ∫ du/dp ds' — the '1.' is probably 'wird' or 'eine' rather than an enumeration.
The final line 'dz = ds e^{du/ds} ... dπ = dσ e^{psi i}, wenn rho, psi die Winkel' is mostly struck; 'dπ' may be 'dz' or 'dt' in the image.
